name: Presence Boundary
summary: Shows what an agent is doing now, what it can access, and how a person can pause or change its scope.

notes.L1: The person operating one agent sees its live state and scope.
notes.L2: Peer agents or an orchestrator receive state and scope as structured data so they can coordinate around the boundary.
notes.L3: The person sees one strip per agent and can pause an agent or narrow its reach.
notes.L4: The team sees each agent's boundary and who paused it or changed its scope.

triggers: It starts long-running work
Its activity changes to idle, observing, working, waiting, or acting
Its observation scope, action scope, or review requirement changes
spec: When the agent's activity or access scope changes, the agent signals to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through chat, and expects them to monitor its boundary or step in.
whatItSolves: A person can follow an agent's work between chat turns and see whether it stays within the scope they set. They can step in when the work or access needs to change.
interactionModel: The agent updates its state as it moves between idle, observing, working, waiting, and acting. A short activity line and state track show the change. The boundary separates information it can observe from things it may change, with any review requirement. A person can pause the agent, narrow its scope, or explicitly widen it; the view then shows the new boundary.

interactionSteps.title: Update activity
interactionSteps.description: Show each move between idle, observing, working, waiting, and acting with a short activity line.

interactionSteps.title: Expose the boundary
interactionSteps.description: Separate what the agent may observe from what it may change, including any review requirement.

interactionSteps.title: Apply a decision
interactionSteps.description: Pause, narrow, or explicitly widen the scope, then show the resulting state and boundary.

whereItEmbeds: A portable primitive: shown on its own, and docked into a host surface wherever the agent already works. With one agent it is a single strip; with several in play, one strip per agent, so a person can pause one or narrow its reach from the same place.
example: One status orb shows the live state with a short activity line. A five-step track places that state on the idle-to-acting spectrum. A scope panel separates watching from can-act-on, with an access level. Pause, Narrow, and Widen steer the boundary.

principles.why: The person can pause the agent or change what it may observe and act on.
The current activity and access boundary stay visible as they change.

name: Activity Record
summary: Keeps a time-ordered account of an agent’s work so a person can review its actions, assumptions, results, and open questions.

notes.L1: The operator follows one agent’s progress in chat and reviews its recorded actions, assumptions, results, and open questions.
notes.L3: The operator reviews a shared timeline across agents, with each event attributed to the agent that produced it.

triggers: The agent starts or advances background work
An action, assumption, tool call, or result is recorded
The operator returns after asynchronous work or opens a completed run for review
spec: When work is underway or a person returns after asynchronous work, the agent signals to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through chat, and expects them to review the record or step in.
whatItSolves: When background work changes a system, a person needs enough history to judge what happened and what still needs attention. A concise, ordered record makes that review possible without replaying raw logs.
interactionModel: As work progresses, the agent records observable events such as tool calls, assumptions, actions, and results, with time, status, and relevant artifact. During active work it can show a short progress view; when work pauses or the operator returns, the same record opens as a fuller timeline with unresolved questions. The operator inspects entries, corrects an assumption, answers a question, or follows the host workflow to reverse or approve an action.

interactionSteps.title: Record observable work
interactionSteps.description: Add tool calls, assumptions, actions, and results to one time-ordered history.

interactionSteps.title: Adjust the detail
interactionSteps.description: Keep active progress brief; open the same history into a fuller timeline for later review.

interactionSteps.title: Review and respond
interactionSteps.description: Inspect an entry, correct an assumption, or answer an unresolved question.

whereItEmbeds: In the agent’s conversation while it works, and in a shared run or incident view that keeps the history available after the session.
example: On INC-2231, the record shows a 5xx spike at 03:08, the agent’s retry-storm assumption at 03:16, replica scaling from 3 to 6 at 03:40, and a pending owner sign-off at 07:00.

principles.why: Actions, assumptions, tool calls, and results stay in a time-ordered record.
The person can see what the agent did and what still needs attention.

name: Inline Rationale
summary: Explains why a specific output or state change occurred, beside the result it explains.

notes.L1: The person sees why one agent produced an output or changed state.
notes.L3: The person sees the rationale beside decisions made by several agents.

triggers: An output is delivered
The system changes state
A person asks why
spec: When it delivers an output or a recommendation, the agent explains to the person using it in a single-agent setup, through chat, and expects them to evaluate the reasoning and verify its sources.
whatItSolves: A person can understand an output at the moment they see it. The explanation sits beside the result or state change it accounts for, where it can inform the next decision.
interactionModel: Attached to a specific output or state change: a short title, the reasoning behind it, a confidence level, and a few labeled rationale lines. Two variants by what's being explained, why this output came out this way, and why the system changed state, each giving the reader a way to acknowledge it or open the fuller trace.

interactionSteps.title: Attach
interactionSteps.description: Place a rationale beside the output or state change it explains.

interactionSteps.title: Explain
interactionSteps.description: Show a short reason, confidence, and labeled rationale lines.

interactionSteps.title: Follow up
interactionSteps.description: Let the reader acknowledge it or open the fuller trace.

whereItEmbeds: Inline in chat, docked to the message it explains, or in a shared UI beside the output or state it accounts for. It travels with its output rather than sitting in a separate reasoning tab.
example: Next to triage's restart proposal: 'Why triage wants to restart payments-svc, the 5xx spike matches a retry storm, and a restart clears the stuck queue without a deploy.' Confidence 68%, reversible: yes.

principles.why: The reason for an output appears beside that output, where the person evaluates it.

name: Structured Finding
summary: Presents a conclusion as a claim with its confidence and supporting sources.

notes.L1: The person reviews one agent's conclusion with its confidence and sources.
notes.L3: The person compares findings from several agents before acting.

triggers: An analysis completes
A diagnosis is handed over
spec: When an analysis completes or a diagnosis is handed over, the agent explains to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through chat, and expects them to evaluate the conclusion and verify its sources.
whatItSolves: A reader can scan a conclusion, judge its certainty, and check its basis without extracting those facts from a paragraph. Each finding puts the claim, confidence, and sources together.
interactionModel: Each finding is a claim with its supporting sources and, where it applies, a confidence level. Three variants by how much certainty is shown: findings with their sources, a diagnostic report that ranks suspected causes by confidence with a recommended action, and a decision with the criteria it was weighed against. The reader evaluates the claim and follows a source to verify it.

interactionSteps.title: State
interactionSteps.description: Present each claim with its supporting sources and, where relevant, confidence.

interactionSteps.title: Compare
interactionSteps.description: Rank suspected causes or show the criteria behind a decision when the variant calls for it.

interactionSteps.title: Verify
interactionSteps.description: Let the reader evaluate the conclusion and follow a source.

whereItEmbeds: In chat when an analysis completes, and lined up in a shared view when several agents' findings need review side by side. The structure is what lets a person compare one agent's conclusion against another's.
example: The night's diagnostic report: 'Checkout retry storm' at 68% (pause the retry job) and 'Replica saturation' at 90% (keep 6 replicas until traffic falls), each with the evidence it rests on.

principles.why: A finding separates its claim, confidence, and evidence for inspection.
Named sources let the receiver check what supports the conclusion.

name: Source Attribution
summary: Shows what a claim is based on so a person or another agent can verify it.

notes.L1: The person reading one agent's claim can follow its cited sources.
notes.L2: Peer agents receive provenance with a claim so they can check it before using it.
notes.L3: The person verifies claims and sources contributed by several agents.

triggers: A claim rests on external data
An agent consumes a peer's output
A person verifies
spec: When a claim rests on external data, the agent explains to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through chat, and expects them to evaluate the claim and verify its sources.
whatItSolves: A person or another agent can check what a claim rests on before relying on it. Provenance travels with the claim instead of being left to trust.
interactionModel: A claim shown with the specific sources behind it, each one followable. The same structure serves two readers: a person checking citations, and an agent consuming a peer's output, where the provenance is how trust is carried between them.

interactionSteps.title: Make a claim
interactionSteps.description: Show the statement in chat, a shared view, or an agent message.

interactionSteps.title: Attach sources
interactionSteps.description: Name the specific evidence behind it and keep each source followable.

interactionSteps.title: Check
interactionSteps.description: Let a person or downstream agent verify the claim before using it.

whereItEmbeds: In chat and shared UIs for a person reading, and in agent-to-agent messages, where provenance travels with the claim so a downstream agent can verify before it relies on it.
example: 'The 5xx spike on payments-svc traces to the checkout retry loop, not a capacity ceiling', shown with the error logs from 03:08-03:12, the retry config in deploy 4f2a, and the replica saturation dashboard.

principles.why: The receiver can see which source supports a particular claim.
The claim retains a checkable path back to its source.

name: Deferred Detail
summary: Shows which decisions remain open in each phase, why they must wait, and what evidence allows the next phase to begin.

notes.L1: One person sees what the agent can decide now, what it has deferred, and the evidence needed to move on.
notes.L3: One person follows open decisions and handoffs across agents as phase ownership changes.
notes.L4: Teams see which group owns each phase and which evidence or decision unlocks the next handoff.

triggers: A new phase begins and the agent names decisions that cannot yet be made
New evidence resolves or changes a deferred decision
A decision gate is reached and ownership passes to the next phase
spec: When a phase begins or evidence makes a deferred decision possible, the agent signals to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through chat, and expects them to monitor what remains open or decide whether the next phase can begin.
whatItSolves: A person can make commitments in stages as evidence arrives. Each phase makes the postponed decisions explicit, explains why they are premature, and shows the condition that will unlock them.
interactionModel: The agent names the current phase, its owner and outcome, and the decisions left open because information is missing. When evidence arrives, it updates the affected decision and its reason rather than silently replacing the earlier assumption. At the phase gate, it shows the result, the decision now possible, and who takes ownership next. The process view follows these changes without exposing every tool call or action.

interactionSteps.title: Name what must wait
interactionSteps.description: At the start of a phase, show the open decision and the information still missing.

interactionSteps.title: Update the decision
interactionSteps.description: When new evidence arrives, show how it changes the earlier assumption and whether the gate is ready.

interactionSteps.title: Pass the phase onward
interactionSteps.description: Record the result, the decision made, and the next owner at the handoff.

whereItEmbeds: In a conversation while one agent moves through phases, and in a shared process view where people follow decision gates and ownership across a longer effort.
example: A payments migration leaves production capacity open during evaluation because there is no representative traffic data. A limited pilot finds peak demand three times higher than expected, allowing the team to set the capacity target before rollout.

principles.why: A decision stays open until the required evidence allows the next phase to begin.
The view names what is pending, why it must wait, and who owns the next gate.

name: Certainty Boundary
summary: Shows which workflow steps follow fixed rules and which rely on agent judgment or generated content.

notes.L1: The operator sees the execution type and review point for each step in one agent's workflow.
notes.L2: Peer agents receive step types and review gates with the workflow they consume.
notes.L3: The operator sees which steps belong to each agent and where a generated handoff needs review.
notes.L4: The team sees the same step boundaries and who owns each review gate.

triggers: A workflow is configured or changed
A run reaches a judgment or generation step
A step's method or review requirement changes during a run
spec: When a workflow is configured or a step's method changes, the agent declares to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through the settings panel, and expects them to inspect the step boundary or revise the workflow.
whatItSolves: An operator can see where a workflow follows a repeatable path and where an agent must interpret or generate. That makes review points explicit before a generated result is used downstream.
interactionModel: The workflow labels each step by how it runs: a fixed API call, an agent-selected path, or generated content. It shows the input and output at each transition and identifies any review gate. As configuration or execution changes the path, the boundary updates. The operator inspects the affected step and reviews generated work at the gate before it continues.

interactionSteps.title: Map the path
interactionSteps.description: Mark each step as fixed, agent-selected, or generated, in the order it runs.

interactionSteps.title: Show the transition
interactionSteps.description: Identify the input, output, and review gate where the workflow moves into generated work.

interactionSteps.title: Update the boundary
interactionSteps.description: When a step changes method or reaches review, show the new path before downstream work continues.

principles.why: The workflow distinguishes fixed rules, agent choice, and generated work.
A person can inspect or revise the steps that require review.

name: Details Dashboard
summary: Keeps the state of one entity or process visible while related work continues.

notes.L1: The person inspects the current state of an entity or process one agent is working on.
notes.L3: The person and agents use the same state view during a review.

triggers: Someone is inspecting an entity, topic or process
spec: When someone is inspecting an entity, topic or process, the agent signals to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through a shared UI, and expects them to monitor its state or step in.
whatItSolves: A person inspecting a service or process can see its current state together, without assembling it from logs, metrics, and chat. That shared view supports a timely decision to step in.
interactionModel: A titled panel for one entity, its headline stats, a row of secondary stats, and a short description. Read-only and always current: a person inspecting a service, a topic, or a process reads its state here and steps in elsewhere if it's wrong.

interactionSteps.title: Select
interactionSteps.description: Open the entity or process being inspected.

interactionSteps.title: Read
interactionSteps.description: Show its headline stats, secondary measures, and a short description together.

interactionSteps.title: Respond
interactionSteps.description: Keep the view current while the person monitors it or steps in elsewhere.

whereItEmbeds: In a shared UI, an incident page, a service view, an entity inspector, wherever one thing is under scrutiny while work goes on around it.
example: payments-svc during the checkout-latency incident: error rate 0.4%, 6 replicas, p99 820ms, with peak 5xx at 4.1% and recovery logged at 03:48.

principles.why: The changing state of one entity or process is visible in a single place.

name: Capability Manifest
summary: Shows an agent's capabilities, limits, alerts, and connection status so people know what it can do before using it.

notes.L1: A person sees one agent's capabilities and whether it is ready.
notes.L2: Peers discover the agent's capabilities and operating limits.
notes.L3: A person can inspect the capabilities of agents working together.
notes.L4: Teams share a view of available agents and their limits.

triggers: An agent initializes or connects
A capability or permission changes
An alert or connection status changes
spec: When an agent initializes or its capabilities change, the agent declares to the person operating it in a single-agent setup, through the settings panel, and expects them to calibrate trust and set scope.
whatItSolves: Before assigning work, a person can see which tasks the agent can handle, which need approval, and which are unavailable. That helps them set the right scope and avoid relying on a capability the agent cannot use.
interactionModel: The agent declares its capabilities and their states, shows conditions, alerts, and connection status, then updates the manifest when those facts change.

interactionSteps.title: Declare
interactionSteps.description: Name the agent and show each capability as available, awaiting approval, restricted, or in error.

interactionSteps.title: Qualify
interactionSteps.description: Show conditions such as read-only access, alerts that affect use, and the live connection state.

interactionSteps.title: Update
interactionSteps.description: Refresh the manifest when availability or permissions change so the person can reassess its scope.

example: A support agent can search tickets and draft replies, but sending a reply awaits approval. Its CRM connection is down, so the manifest shows the affected capability as unavailable before anyone assigns it work.

principles.why: A person can use declared capabilities and limits to set the agent's scope.
Connection, availability, and approval requirements are visible before work starts.

name: Credential Boundary
summary: Divides access across agents when a task needs data or permissions that no single agent should hold.

notes.L2: Peer agents reason within separate access scopes and exchange conclusions through a broker.
notes.L3: The operator sets scoped access before work, reviews the combined conclusions, and resolves any remaining gap without pooling restricted data.

triggers: A task needs data no single agent may hold
Partial conclusions conflict
spec: When a task needs data no single agent may hold, the agent coordinates with its peer agents and the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through a shared record, and expects the operator to set scoped access and resolve any gaps without pooling access.
whatItSolves: Agents can complete work that spans restricted data while each stays within its own access. They coordinate on conclusions without pooling the underlying data or expanding any one agent's permissions.
interactionModel: The operator sets separate access scopes before work begins. Agents reason in parallel on only the data they may hold and coordinate through a policy broker that passes conclusions, never raw data. The operator reviews the combined conclusions and resolves any remaining gap without pooling restricted inputs.

interactionSteps.title: Set scopes
interactionSteps.description: The operator assigns each agent only the data and tools within its permitted scope.

interactionSteps.title: Coordinate
interactionSteps.description: Pass conclusions through a policy broker without sharing restricted inputs.

interactionSteps.title: Review gaps
interactionSteps.description: The operator reviews the combined conclusions and resolves any open gap without pooling access.

whereItEmbeds: Runs between agents that must stay separated, in a shared record or broker surface the operator uses to set scopes and review conclusions. Pairs with Shared Cognitive State, which holds the common picture the partitioned agents still need.
example: The operator gives a fraud agent an AML scope and a credit agent a lending scope. They coordinate through a policy broker; the operator reviews their combined conclusions without either agent receiving the other's raw data.

principles.why: Access stays scoped instead of being pooled across agents.
Agents coordinate across the boundary while the operator resolves access gaps.

name: Convergence Point
summary: Shows how several agents reached an answer so a person can review the evidence and resolve any remaining disagreement.

notes.L2: Peer agents weigh conflicting answers and adopt one or flag an impasse.
notes.L3: The operator reviews how the agents weighed evidence, accepts or reopens the adopted answer, and settles an impasse.

triggers: Sub-agents disagree
An answer is adopted
An impasse is escalated
spec: When sub-agents reach conflicting answers, the agent resolves with its peer agents and the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through a shared record, and expects the operator to review the adopted answer or settle an impasse.
whatItSolves: Agents and people can see how a shared answer was reached, including the evidence weighed and any unresolved conflict. That account makes the adopted answer possible to examine or overturn.
interactionModel: The conflicting agents are shown together and their sources are scored. The resolver adopts an answer with its reasoning attached, or flags an impasse when nothing can be adopted. The operator reviews the evidence and reasoning, accepts or reopens the adopted answer, or settles the impasse.

interactionSteps.title: Surface conflict
interactionSteps.description: Show the agents' differing answers and the sources behind each.

interactionSteps.title: Weigh
interactionSteps.description: Compare the evidence and attach reasoning to the candidate answer.

interactionSteps.title: Review the result
interactionSteps.description: The operator accepts or reopens the adopted answer, or settles a flagged impasse.

whereItEmbeds: Runs where sub-agents disagree and an answer has to be chosen, in a shared record the operator uses to review the evidence and decision. Sits downstream of Assumption Surface, which explains why they differ before anything is adopted.
example: A panel compares agent A's logs with agent B's code findings. The resolver scores the sources and recommends rollback; the operator reviews the reasoning and accepts it or reopens the conflict.

principles.why: Agents bring conflicting answers together for an adopted answer or an impasse.
The operator can review the evidence and reasoning behind that result.

name: Pre-Action Handshake
summary: The agent presents a proposed action or available actions and waits for a person to choose and authorize what happens next.

notes.L1: The person reviews one agent's proposal or chooses an available action before authorizing it.
notes.L3: The operator reviews actions informed by several agents, with the proposing agent responsible for the handoff.

triggers: The agent detects a signal that may require consequential action
Several available actions need a person to choose what happens next
Immediately before an irreversible or externally visible step
New evidence materially changes the interpretation or proposed action while awaiting a response
spec: When a proposed action or a choice of available actions needs authorization, the agent proposes to the operator in a single-agent setup, through chat, and expects consent to the chosen action, a correction, a decline, or a deferral.
whatItSolves: A person can control what happens next before the agent changes an external system. The context, available actions, and consequences stay visible together so they can make an informed choice and authorize only the action they intend.
interactionModel: The agent presents its observation, interpretation, and either one proposed action or a list of available actions, with affected resources and consequences. The person reviews the proposal or selects an action, then explicitly authorizes it, corrects the plan, declines, or defers. Selecting an option alone does not authorize execution. The agent records the response and performs only the authorized action; a correction or material change to the proposal requires a fresh decision. An irreversible action may require stronger confirmation, such as typing the affected resource name, before authorization is accepted.

interactionSteps.title: Present the actions
interactionSteps.description: Explain the context and show one proposal or the available actions, with their consequences.

interactionSteps.title: Choose and authorize
interactionSteps.description: Let the person review or select an action, then authorize it, correct the plan, decline, or defer.

interactionSteps.title: Apply the decision
interactionSteps.description: Perform only the authorized action; keep declined or deferred work stopped and ask again if the proposal changes.

whereItEmbeds: In the conversation where the agent asks what to do next. The proposal or action list stays attached to the context and consequences, and a changed proposal returns to the same decision point.
example: The Reliability agent sees checkout-api errors rise after release 2.18.5. It proposes rolling back to 2.18.4, or offers rollback, restart, and continued monitoring with their consequences. The operator selects an action and authorizes it, corrects the plan to inspect the canary cohort first, declines, or defers. The preview records the decision locally without changing production.

principles.why: The agent waits for consent, correction, decline, or deferral before acting.
It states what it noticed, how it interpreted the signal, and what it proposes.

name: Assumption Surface
summary: Shows what each agent observed, assumed, and concluded so a person can understand why their answers differ.

notes.L3: The person compares the agents' assumptions and corrects the one behind their disagreement.

triggers: Two agents reach different answers
Before anyone decides which answer to adopt
spec: When two agents reach different answers, and before anyone decides which to adopt, the agent explains to the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through a shared UI, and expects them to correct a wrong assumption, after which the interpretation resting on it is marked stale rather than silently rewritten.
whatItSolves: A person can locate the assumption behind agents' conflicting conclusions and correct it before an answer is adopted. The affected interpretation is marked stale so the change remains visible.
interactionModel: Retrospective, and read mostly. The agents are shown side by side, each with the context it held, the assumption it made, and the interpretation it drew. Assumptions are the only actionable layer: correct one, and the interpretation resting on it is marked stale rather than silently rewritten. There is no approve or reject, approval belongs to Pre-Action Handshake and Authority Gradient.

interactionSteps.title: Compare
interactionSteps.description: Place each agent's context, assumption, and interpretation side by side.

interactionSteps.title: Correct
interactionSteps.description: Let the person change a wrong assumption without approving either conclusion.

interactionSteps.title: Mark stale
interactionSteps.description: Flag the interpretation built on that assumption instead of silently rewriting it.

whereItEmbeds: Opens once agents have already reached different answers and someone needs to know why before deciding anything. Sits upstream of Convergence Point, which handles what gets adopted. Lives inside a case or incident surface, where the chrome already carries the account, the ticket, and who is working it.
example: A refund agent assumed the dispute covers one charge. A subscriptions agent assumed the plan renewed on the old card. Same account, opposite conclusions.

principles.why: The exchange shows what each agent saw, assumed, and concluded.
That shared view gives agents and people a basis for resolving disagreement.

name: Decision Record
summary: Records why the agent chose an action as it commits, so people can review the reason later.

notes.L3: The agent drafts its reason; the operator adds context or commits the decision.
notes.L4: The team can read who approved the decision and why.

triggers: An action is proposed for commit
The operator commits, amends or declines
An audit asks how it was decided
spec: When an action is proposed for commit, the agent commits to the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through a shared UI, and expects them to commit it, add context, or decline.
whatItSolves: A later reviewer can see why an action was approved, including the alternatives considered and the operator's judgment. The reasoning is captured when the decision is made, while it is still available.
interactionModel: Before an action commits, the agent presents it with its stated reason, the alternatives it considered, and the policy version in force. The operator can accept the reason as written or amend it. An amendment does not overwrite: the agent's reason and the operator's revision are both stored, which makes visible the cases where the operator proceeded for a different reason than the agent proposed. On commit the record seals, later readers query it, they do not add to it.

interactionSteps.title: Propose
interactionSteps.description: Show the action, agent's reason, alternatives, and policy version before commit.

interactionSteps.title: Review
interactionSteps.description: Let the operator commit, add context, or decline while preserving both reasons.

interactionSteps.title: Seal
interactionSteps.description: Make the committed record read-only for later review and export.

whereItEmbeds: The approval step of a change record, not a separate audit tool. The record is written where the decision is already being made, which is the only place the rationale exists. Compliance export reads the sealed records and reformats them; it never asks anyone to supply reasoning after the fact.
example: The agent proposes firmware 4.12 on edge-router-7 under CHG-2231, stating that 4.11 has an open memory leak affecting svc-payments. The operator amends the reason: the upgrade is going ahead now because the rollback window closes at month end. Commit stores the agent's reason, the operator's revision, and the policy version that permitted an unattended push.

principles.why: The committed action keeps the agent's reason and any operator amendment.
The operator can amend the reason before the record is sealed.

name: Review as Dialogue
summary: Turns feedback on an agent’s draft into a focused exchange that guides its next revision.

notes.L3: The operator judges whether the Research agent's proposal and the Marketing agent's draft fit the campaign, then steers the revision; Marketing carries that decision into the next draft.

triggers: An agent presents a draft or output for review
The reviewer declines or redirects it and gives a reason
The agent returns with a revision or needs one clarification before revising
spec: When an agent presents a draft or output for review, the agent proposes to the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through chat, and expects consent, a correction, a decline, or a deferral.
whatItSolves: A reviewer can apply context the agents may not know, such as which audience or priority matters for this work. A reasoned response lets the responsible agent clarify, revise, and return the draft for another decision.
interactionModel: A contributing agent may propose a direction, and the responsible agent presents a draft with the decision it needs from the operator. The operator applies contextual judgment about audience, priorities, or fit, then can consent, correct the draft directly, decline with a reason, or defer. When feedback is incomplete, the responsible agent asks one focused clarification; it then revises the draft and makes the changes visible for another review. Each response applies to the current version, so a new revision returns to pending review rather than inheriting an earlier approval.

interactionSteps.title: Present the proposal
interactionSteps.description: Show the contributing agent's recommendation, the current draft, and the contextual decision reserved for the operator.

interactionSteps.title: Steer with feedback
interactionSteps.description: Consent, correct, decline with a reason, or defer; ask one focused question when the feedback needs clarification.

interactionSteps.title: Return for review
interactionSteps.description: Show the revision and what changed, then wait for a fresh decision on that version.

whereItEmbeds: In the agent’s conversation beside the draft under review. Co-editing Surface owns direct edits and comments inside a shared artifact; Review as Dialogue handles a review turn and the agent’s response. If the draft becomes a consequential action, Pre-Action Handshake holds that action for a fresh decision; Decision Record can preserve the rationale when the action is committed.
example: The Research agent recommends leading with a quick setup promise for new trial users, based on survey synthesis. The Marketing agent uses it in a launch email draft. Before scheduling or sending, the operator must judge whether the audience and lead promise fit the campaign. The operator says the draft still reads as aimed at existing customers. Marketing asks whether to emphasize setup time or product value; the operator chooses setup time. Marketing returns a revised draft, marks the audience and opening paragraph as changed, and waits for a fresh decision.

principles.why: A declined draft can return as a clarified, marked revision for another decision.
The person and agent exchange focused feedback instead of ending at rejection.

name: Memory Commitment Review
summary: When an agent changes its position during a session, a person can keep the new belief, restore the earlier one, or leave it out of long-term memory.

notes.L3: The memory owner reviews each belief before it reaches long-term memory.
notes.L4: The memory owner decides whether reviewed beliefs belong in personal, project, or team memory.

triggers: A belief goes stale mid-session
A session ends and its learning is committed
spec: When a session ends and its learning is about to become long-term memory, the agent commits to the person who owns that memory in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through the settings panel, and expects each belief to be kept, restored, or revoked before it is sealed.
whatItSolves: A person can see which beliefs were superseded during a session and decide what should become lasting memory. Stale reasoning stays traceable instead of quietly carrying forward.
interactionModel: Staleness shows inline as beliefs are displaced: a superseded belief appears with the belief that replaced it and a note on what caused the shift, and attribution is preserved, a person sees which agent held which belief and which agent changed it. At the commitment boundary, when session reasoning becomes durable memory, a person reviews each belief and chooses to keep it, restore it (if the update was wrong), or revoke it (exclude it from long-term memory). Their choice is logged as part of the commitment record.

interactionSteps.title: Mark change
interactionSteps.description: Show a superseded belief beside its replacement, cause, and agent attribution.

interactionSteps.title: Review memory
interactionSteps.description: At session end, let the person keep, restore, or revoke each belief.

interactionSteps.title: Commit
interactionSteps.description: Log those choices before the reviewed beliefs become long-term memory.

whereItEmbeds: At two points: in real-time reasoning, when agents update positions and prior beliefs become stale, and at the memory boundary, when a person gates what gets committed to long-term memory. Both are load-bearing moments in multi-agent handoff.
example: A finance agent priced off a 12% churn baseline. Customer Success validated a 41% baseline across 1,200 accounts, so the 12% is marked stale and shown alongside what replaced it. At session end, the person keeps, restores, or revokes each belief before it reaches long-term memory.

principles.why: A person can restore or revoke a changed belief before it becomes durable memory.
The person decides which beliefs the agent may keep across sessions.

name: Disclosure Gradient
summary: The agent leads with the result and reveals its reasoning, agent coordination, and full trace as a person asks for more.

notes.L3: The operator sees the incident outcome first, then opens the reasoning and agent coordination when needed.
notes.L4: The incident response team can inspect the same trace during a postmortem without making every agent visible during live work.

triggers: A result is delivered during active work
The result or status changes during the incident
The operator asks why the result was reached or which agents contributed
A postmortem reviewer opens the full trace
spec: When a result is delivered, the agent signals to the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through chat, and expects them to monitor the outcome or step in for the trace.
whatItSolves: An operator can act on a clear result without sorting through every agent and decision behind it. When they need to check the basis or investigate later, the reasoning, coordination, and full trace remain available in layers.
interactionModel: The agent presents the outcome and its operational status first. The operator can open the rationale, then inspect which agents contributed and how work moved between them, then open the full trace for a postmortem. New material changes the outcome or status in place; expanded layers remain available to explain the update.

interactionSteps.title: Lead with outcome
interactionSteps.description: Show the result and current status in the live conversation, with no agent roster or trace in the default view.

interactionSteps.title: Reveal on request
interactionSteps.description: Let the operator open the rationale and agent handoffs when they ask how the result was reached.

interactionSteps.title: Inspect the trace
interactionSteps.description: Keep the full sequence available for a deeper check or postmortem, and update the visible result when the work changes.

example: The incident agent reports, “Incident mitigated.” The operator opens Why to see that a database agent identified a connection pool spike and a remediation agent restarted the affected service, then opens Full trace to inspect the evidence and event order during review.

principles.why: The result leads, while rationale, coordination, and the full trace remain available on request.

name: Co-Editing Surface
summary: A person and multiple agents revise the same document in a shared workspace.

notes.L3: The operator and several agents work from the same document, with each change attributed to its author.
notes.L4: Several people or teams and their agents revise the shared document, with changes attributed across the group.

triggers: An agent creates an editable document for the operator and other agents
The person changes the document in place
The person comments on a specific part of the document
Another agent revises the document after the person's contribution
A participant returns to the current document
spec: When a shared document is created or revised, the agent coordinates with the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through a shared UI, and expects them to edit or comment on its parts before another agent continues.
whatItSolves: Keep the work in one document so the operator can revise an agent's draft or comment on a specific part before another agent continues. Everyone sees the current text, its comments, and who contributed to each change.
interactionModel: An agent drafts a document in the shared workspace or attaches it to a conversation. The operator edits its text or attaches a comment to a named part. Another agent reads those contributions, adds a section to the same document, and preserves the operator's edits and comments. The current text, comments, and attribution remain visible as work continues.

interactionSteps.title: Draft
interactionSteps.description: One agent writes the first version of a shared document.

interactionSteps.title: Revise or comment
interactionSteps.description: The operator edits text or comments on a specific document part.

interactionSteps.title: Continue
interactionSteps.description: Another agent adds to the document while keeping the operator's edits and comments attached.

whereItEmbeds: In a shared document workspace or as an editable document attached to an agent reply.
example: The Incident agent drafts a restart-plan document for payments-svc. The operator changes the proposed action and comments on what to watch. The Reliability agent adds an impact assessment to that same document while preserving the edit and comment.

principles.why: A person and several agents revise the same document in one shared workspace.
Each contribution remains attributed to its author.

name: Concurrent Workspace Awareness
summary: Helps agents distinguish a person’s feedback or override from unrelated edits in a shared workspace.

notes.L3: The agent interprets live human edits.

triggers: A person edits while the agent drafts
spec: When a person edits while it is drafting, the agent coordinates with the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through a shared UI, and expects them to act jointly on the same artifact.
whatItSolves: In a shared workspace, an edit can look like a signal to an agent even when it was made for another reason. Marking feedback and overrides explicitly helps the agent respond to the change the person intended.

principles.why: Agents interpret live human edits as feedback, override, or unrelated work.
A person's edit can redirect the agent's work in progress.

name: Authority Gradient
summary: Sets a separate autonomy level for each workflow area, matching authority to risk.

notes.L3: The operator sets an autonomy level for each area the agents work in.
notes.L4: The team sees which roles can change authority in each area.

triggers: Setup, before work starts
The agent hits the edge of its authority
The risk level of an area changes
spec: When work is being set up or the agent reaches its authority boundary, the agent declares to the operator in a multi-agent system with one person in the loop, through the settings panel, and expects them to set or adjust the autonomy level for that workflow area.
whatItSolves: An operator can grant routine work more independence while keeping sensitive work under closer review. Each workflow area gets an autonomy level matched to its risk.
interactionModel: For each workflow area, the operator sets one of four levels: Suggest, Ask first, Act + review, or Act alone. Each row shows its risk tone and who set the level. Operators can adjust a level in place as the workflow or its risk changes, without pausing the agent.

interactionSteps.title: Set levels
interactionSteps.description: Choose Suggest, Ask first, Act + review, or Act alone for each workflow area.

interactionSteps.title: Show boundaries
interactionSteps.description: Display each area's risk tone and who set its current level.

interactionSteps.title: Adjust
interactionSteps.description: Change a level when risk shifts or decide when the agent reaches its boundary.

whereItEmbeds: Primary: agent settings or an orchestration console, where levels are set before work starts. Secondary: inline in the inbox when an agent reaches a boundary mid-task and needs a decision. It pairs with Presence Boundary for action scope and Review as Dialogue for areas set to act-with-review.
example: Acme Renewal, Finance Agent: approve discount (Act + review), escalate to Director (Ask first). Customer Success: validate churn signals (Act + review). Each row shows its risk tone and who set the level.

principles.why: A person sets a separate autonomy level for each workflow area.

name: Lineage View
summary: Shows what claims, artifacts and decisions depend on a given agent output.

notes.L2: Peer agents can trace which outputs they cite before passing a dependent result onward.
notes.L3: A sales lead can inspect work across agents and hold a promotion that relies on a disputed count.
notes.L4: Sales, fulfillment, and marketing teams see what relies on the same count and can coordinate review before the sale launches.

triggers: An upstream output is disputed or goes stale
Before approving work that relies on the output
spec: When an upstream output is disputed or goes stale, the agent explains to every team that relies on it in a multi-agent system shared by several teams, through a shared UI, and expects them to verify the blast radius before acting.
whatItSolves: Teams can see which claims, artifacts, and decisions rely on a disputed or stale agent output, so they can check the source and coordinate review before dependent work proceeds.
interactionModel: The shared incident workspace highlights the disputed or stale source with its claim, the evidence challenging it, its author, and last verification time. It lists all affected decisions and artifacts with their producing agents and whether they rely on the source directly or through another item. Selecting an item reveals its full dependency path and the review needed before that work proceeds. The summary counts affected items, decisions, and teams.

interactionSteps.title: Explain the dispute
interactionSteps.description: Show the reported count, the conflicting recount, and when each was known.

interactionSteps.title: Review affected work
interactionSteps.description: List every dependent item with its agent and direct or indirect reliance.

interactionSteps.title: Trace a path
interactionSteps.description: Select an item to see how it depends on the source and what needs review.

example: In the SALE-104 workspace, the Inventory agent reports 120 Trail Bottles available for a weekend sale. A warehouse recount finds only 12 saleable units even though no stock moved, putting that count under dispute. The Sales agent's promotion decision and the Fulfillment agent's 100-unit allocation both use the count directly. The Marketing agent's launch email draft follows the promotion decision. Three teams need to review their work before the sale launches.

principles.why: Claims, artifacts, and decisions can be traced back through their dependencies.
A questioned source reveals which downstream work needs review.

name: Shared Cognitive State
summary: Keeps goals, assumptions, conflicts, and open questions visible to people and agents working together.
triggers: Work spans teams or org boundaries
A conflict is flagged before execution
spec: When work spans teams or org boundaries, the agent coordinates with the teams involved in a multi-agent system shared by several teams, through a shared UI, and expects them to act jointly on shared goals, assumptions and conflicts.
whatItSolves: When people and agents work together, goals, assumptions, conflicts, and open questions can drift apart. A shared state gives everyone one place to check the current understanding and update it as the work changes.

principles.why: People and agents coordinate around shared goals, assumptions, conflicts, and open questions.
The common view makes those working assumptions visible to the participants.

name: Workshop Card
summary: Coordinates a group around a scheduled session: who is attending, and where each of them stands.

notes.L4: The group sees the session details, attendees, and confirmation status together.

triggers: An agent schedules or coordinates a group
spec: When it schedules or coordinates a group, the agent coordinates with the teams involved in a multi-agent system shared by several teams, through chat, and expects them to act jointly.
whatItSolves: A group can see the session details, who is attending, and its confirmation state together. Everyone reads the same current plan instead of piecing it together from invites and messages.
interactionModel: A card for one scheduled session: its type, time, duration and location, the attendee list with a count, and a confirmation status. It coordinates a group, everyone reads the same card and sees where the others are.

interactionSteps.title: Schedule
interactionSteps.description: Show the session type, time, duration, and location.

interactionSteps.title: Gather
interactionSteps.description: List attendees and their count on the same shared card.

interactionSteps.title: Confirm
interactionSteps.description: Update the session status so the group can see where it stands.

whereItEmbeds: In chat where the group is already talking, and in a shared UI for a session several people or teams need to track. It opens when an agent schedules or coordinates a group.
example: Incident retro for INC-2231: a 45-minute postmortem on Oct 7 at 10:00 in the war room, with the on-call engineer, service owner, and SRE lead among four attendees, status confirmed.

principles.why: A group can see who is attending a session and where each participant stands.

name: Stream of Thought
summary: The agent shows its reasoning as it unfolds, so a person can follow or interrupt before a conclusion lands.

notes.L1: The person following one agent sees its reasoning step by step.
notes.L3: The operator can scroll back, interrupt, or redirect as the reasoning unfolds.

triggers: The agent begins a multi-step task
A reasoning step changes direction mid-task
The agent is about to commit to a conclusion
spec: When it begins or changes direction during a multi-step task, the agent signals to the person operating it in a system with many agents and one person in the loop, through chat, and expects them to follow, interrupt, or redirect.
whatItSolves: A person can follow the agent's reasoning as it happens and interrupt before the wrong conclusion lands. Useful when the task has several steps and the agent's path is not obvious.
interactionModel: The agent's reasoning appears progressively in the chat. Each new step is marked and earlier steps stay visible. The person can scroll back or interrupt; the agent acknowledges the interrupt, pauses, and continues from the new point.

interactionSteps.title: Begin
interactionSteps.description: Open a reasoning stream marked as ongoing when the task starts.

interactionSteps.title: Reveal
interactionSteps.description: Add each step as it is reasoned, keeping earlier steps visible.

interactionSteps.title: Yield
interactionSteps.description: Pause on interrupt or acknowledge a redirect, then continue from the new point.

whereItEmbeds: In the agent's conversation, as a live reasoning stream that sits above the next action. Pairs with Inline Rationale, which attaches a condensed explanation to the final output.
example: On INC-2231, the Reliability agent streams: 'Examining 5xx spike around 03:08 → correlates with deploy 4f2a at 03:04 → candidate cause: new retry policy → checking retry count spike…' and the operator interrupts to narrow the check to one service.

principles.why: The agent's reasoning appears as it unfolds, where a person can read it.
A person can interrupt or redirect before the agent commits.

name: Follow Up
summary: The agent asks one focused clarifying question when the request is ambiguous, rather than guessing.

notes.L3: The operator answers the single question or explicitly skips it.

triggers: The request is ambiguous and the agent cannot infer the missing fact
Required context is missing before the agent can act
spec: When a request is ambiguous or required context is missing, the agent requests from the person operating it in a system with many agents and one person in the loop, through chat, and expects an answer or an explicit skip.
whatItSolves: The agent gets the context it needs before acting, with one focused question rather than guessing. The person is not asked for information the agent already has.
interactionModel: The agent identifies what it does not know and composes one focused question. It poses the question and waits. The person answers or explicitly skips; the agent proceeds with the answer or with a stated assumption.

interactionSteps.title: Identify the gap
interactionSteps.description: Name the specific missing fact the agent cannot infer from context.

interactionSteps.title: Ask one question
interactionSteps.description: Pose a focused question rather than a list, and wait for the answer.

interactionSteps.title: Use the answer
interactionSteps.description: Incorporate the answer, or proceed with a stated assumption on skip.

whereItEmbeds: In the agent's conversation at the moment it discovers the gap. Distinct from Pre-Action Handshake, which pauses before a consequential action; Follow Up pauses because the agent cannot proceed without a fact.
example: On a draft reply to a billing dispute, the agent asks: 'Does this dispute cover one charge or the whole series?' The operator says 'the whole series', and the agent revises the draft to address all affected transactions.

principles.why: The agent asks about the specific missing fact instead of guessing.
The person's answer, or an explicit skip, decides what the agent does next.

name: Memory
summary: The agent keeps relevant facts across turns and sessions, with the person able to see and change what it remembers.

notes.L1: The person sees what the agent has learned about them over time.
notes.L3: The operator reviews proposed memory entries and can edit or forget any of them.

triggers: The agent learns a durable fact about the person or their work
The person opens their memory settings
A memory entry would change the agent's behavior
spec: When the agent learns a durable fact or the person opens their memory, the agent declares to the person operating it in a system with many agents and one person in the loop, through the settings panel, and expects them to keep, edit, or forget the entry.
whatItSolves: The agent remembers what matters across sessions, and the person sees exactly what it holds, with the ability to change or remove any entry.
interactionModel: The agent proposes a memory entry when it learns something durable, with a quick inline accept in chat. The full memory list is available in settings: each entry shows what the agent remembers, when it was learned, and controls to edit or forget it.

interactionSteps.title: Propose
interactionSteps.description: When learning a durable fact, show a one-line entry the person can accept inline.

interactionSteps.title: List
interactionSteps.description: Keep the full memory accessible in settings, with each entry traceable to its source.

interactionSteps.title: Change
interactionSteps.description: Let the person edit or forget any entry; the agent adapts from that point on.

whereItEmbeds: Inline in chat as single-line proposals and in settings as the durable memory list. Pairs with Memory Commitment Review for session-end gating of what reaches long-term memory.
example: After an operator says 'we rarely restart during business hours', the agent proposes: 'Remembered: prefers to avoid restarts during business hours.' The operator accepts; later, when a restart comes up at 2pm, the agent asks first.

principles.why: The person can keep, edit, or forget any memory entry.
Each memory entry is traceable to when and where the agent learned it.

name: Task Creation
summary: The agent turns a request into a named task with an owner and an expected result.

notes.L3: The operator reviews the proposed task, edits any field, and accepts or declines.
notes.L4: Teams see created tasks alongside other work, with the proposing agent attributed.

triggers: A request implies work that spans multiple steps
A person asks the agent to track something
A conversation produces a commitment that should not be lost
spec: When a request implies multi-step work, the agent proposes to the person operating it in a system with many agents and one person in the loop, through a shared UI, and expects them to accept, edit, or decline the task.
whatItSolves: A person can turn a request into a tracked task with a clear owner and expected result, instead of having the work disappear into the conversation.
interactionModel: The agent proposes a task card with name, expected result, and owner. The person accepts it as-is, edits the fields, or declines. Accepted tasks are tracked where the person can see them alongside other work.

interactionSteps.title: Propose a task
interactionSteps.description: Suggest a name, expected result, and owner derived from the request.

interactionSteps.title: Edit before accept
interactionSteps.description: Let the person adjust any field before the task is created.

interactionSteps.title: Track
interactionSteps.description: Put accepted tasks where the person can see them alongside other work.

whereItEmbeds: In chat as a card and in a shared task view where accepted tasks accumulate. Pairs with Subtask Generation when the proposed task is itself a container.
example: After an operator says 'investigate the checkout retries', the agent proposes a task: 'Investigate checkout retry storm · Expected result: root cause and fix plan · Owner: @triage'. The operator accepts; the task appears in the incident workspace.

principles.why: A request becomes a shared task with a visible owner and expected result.
The person edits or declines the proposal before the task is tracked.

name: Task Assignment
summary: The agent assigns a task to a peer agent whose capabilities match, and shows who owns what.

notes.L2: Peer agents coordinate assignments against each other's capability manifests, without a person routing every task.
notes.L3: The operator sees the transfer in the shared view and can reassign if needed.

triggers: A task matches another agent's declared capability
The current agent hits its own capability boundary
A peer accepts, declines, or asks for clarification
spec: When a task matches a peer agent's capability, the agent delegates to its peer agents in a system with many agents and no person in the loop, through a message to another agent, and expects an accept, a decline, or a request for clarification.
whatItSolves: Work reaches the agent best suited to do it, without a person routing every task. Responsibility is explicit, and the shared view shows who owns what.
interactionModel: The assigning agent picks a peer whose declared capability matches and sends the task with enough context for the peer to decide. The peer accepts, declines with a reason, or asks for clarification. Accepted tasks move into the peer's workload and the shared view reflects the transfer.

interactionSteps.title: Match
interactionSteps.description: Pick a peer whose declared capability matches the task.

interactionSteps.title: Send
interactionSteps.description: Pass the task with enough context for the peer to decide.

interactionSteps.title: Transfer
interactionSteps.description: On accept, move the task to the peer and update the shared view.

whereItEmbeds: Between agents as structured messages and in a shared task view for the operator. Sits downstream of Capability Manifest, which supplies the matching data, and alongside Task Creation, which produces what gets assigned.
example: The Triage agent assigns 'produce a 72-hour deploy diff' to the Reliability agent whose capability manifest lists deploy comparison. Reliability accepts; the task moves into its queue and the shared incident view shows the new owner.

principles.why: Peer agents coordinate who does what through structured accept or decline.
The shared view records who owns each assignment.

name: Priority Ranking
summary: The agent orders tasks by weight and lets a person see and adjust the ranking.

notes.L3: The operator sees the ranking with a reason per task and can reorder it.
notes.L4: Teams see one ranking that reflects the group's priorities, with changes attributed.

triggers: Several tasks are in flight
The person opens the task list
A new task arrives that changes the ranking
spec: When several tasks are in flight, the agent declares to the person operating it in a system with many agents and one person in the loop, through a shared UI, and expects them to accept the ranking or reorder it.
whatItSolves: A person sees which task the agent plans to do next and why, with the ability to override. Work is not implicitly prioritized by order of arrival.
interactionModel: The agent ranks pending tasks by its own weighting, including deadline, blocker status, and impact. It shows the ranking with a short reason per task. The person can accept the order or drag to reorder; the agent updates its own weighting from the overrides.

interactionSteps.title: Rank
interactionSteps.description: Order pending tasks with a short reason attached to each.

interactionSteps.title: Show
interactionSteps.description: Present the ranking where the person can see and inspect it.

interactionSteps.title: Learn from overrides
interactionSteps.description: Update the agent's own weighting when the person reorders.

whereItEmbeds: In a shared task view, inline with the task list. Pairs with Task Creation and Subtask Generation, which produce the items being ranked, and with Memory when the overrides should carry across sessions.
example: Three tasks pending: fix broken build (blocker, one person waiting), update docs (deadline this week), renew certificate (expires in 3 days). The agent ranks: fix build, renew cert, update docs. The operator moves cert above build.

principles.why: The agent's reason for each rank is visible beside the task.
A person can reorder the list and the agent learns from the override.

name: Subtask Generation
summary: The agent breaks a complex task into subtasks and shows how they combine into the overall result.

notes.L3: The operator reviews the proposed subtasks and can edit, reorder, or remove any of them.
notes.L4: Teams see the breakdown and who owns each subtask once accepted.

triggers: A task is too complex for one step
A person asks to break down a task
A peer agent returns a task as too broad to accept
spec: When a task is too complex for one step, the agent proposes to the person operating it in a system with many agents and one person in the loop, through a shared UI, and expects them to accept the subtasks, edit them, or decline.
whatItSolves: A complex task becomes a small set of defined subtasks a person can review before work begins, instead of being handed off as one opaque job.
interactionModel: The agent breaks the task into an ordered set of subtasks with expected results and marks any dependencies. The person reviews, edits any subtask, reorders them, or removes some. On accept, the subtasks become trackable children of the parent task.

interactionSteps.title: Break down
interactionSteps.description: Propose an ordered set of subtasks with expected results.

interactionSteps.title: Show dependencies
interactionSteps.description: Mark which subtasks depend on which others so review knows the order.

interactionSteps.title: Accept as work
interactionSteps.description: On accept, the subtasks are tracked as children of the parent task.

whereItEmbeds: In a shared task view, nested under the parent task. Pairs with Task Creation, which makes the parent, and Task Assignment, which routes each subtask to a peer when needed.
example: For 'reduce checkout p99 latency', the agent proposes: measure current p99 by endpoint, identify the top two slow endpoints, profile them, propose fixes with risk notes, measure after. The operator edits the fixes subtask to require risk notes.

principles.why: A person and the agent review the breakdown before any subtask is tracked.
Dependencies between subtasks are marked where review can see them.

name: Disclosure
summary: Labels AI-generated content so people know when they are interacting with an AI.
what: A persistent visual or textual indicator that any response, suggestion, or action is generated by a machine: not authored by a human.
why: Clear attribution helps people understand when they are interacting with AI.
when: At the first AI interaction and wherever an AI-generated response or action appears.
how: Place a clear label beside the assistant name, the first-use explanation, or the generated content.
code:
Made with AI

AI-generated content may contain errors. Check it before use.

placements.note: Sits in the message header beside the agent name so attribution is visible on every turn.
Anchored at the top of the assistant panel on first open. Establishes the contract before the person types.
Below every generated asset on the canvas so anything exported carries provenance.
On AI-generated clips in the timeline: a small AI tag makes machine-made segments scannable in the edit.
Beside the inline assistant prompt in the editor so developers know they're talking to the agent, not a teammate.
Label an AI-drafted reply before the person sends it.

variants.name: Header AI badge
variants.note: Lightest touch. A small chip beside the agent name in the message header: visible at every turn without taking attention.

variants.name: Footer attribution line
variants.note: A short caption under the message: who generated it, what to do with it. Most useful when output will be acted on or shared.

variants.name: Persistent input-area chip
variants.note: Sits above or beside the composer. Tells the person every turn from this surface goes to an AI, not a person.

variants.name: First-run banner
variants.note: Heavier disclosure for the first session: explains what this is, links to the policy, dismissible. Used once per person.

name: Consent
summary: Asks before collecting or using a person’s data for training.
what: A blocking dialog (or progressive disclosure card) at sign-up or first sensitive interaction that asks the person to grant or deny use of their data.
why: People need to know what data is collected and choose whether it can be used for training.
when: Ask when a person first signs up or connects a service, and whenever the terms for data use change.
how: Explain what data will be used and why. Offer equally clear choices to allow or decline, link to the full policy, and avoid dark patterns.
code:
Allow the assistant to use your data?

Choose how your data can be used. See the privacy policy for details.

Read the privacy policy

placements.note: Appears on first send so the person opts in before any data leaves the device.
Sits at the top of the panel the first time the assistant needs context from the workspace.
Required acknowledgement before the first generative action on the canvas.
Tucked into preferences so developers control telemetry without breaking flow.
Inline in the compose window before the AI drafts on the person's behalf.

variants.name: Blocking modal
variants.note: centered dialog the person must respond to before continuing. Used the first time data leaves the device.

variants.name: Inline progressive card
variants.note: A consent card embedded directly in the flow: less disruptive than a modal, used for non-blocking permissions.

variants.name: Settings toggle
variants.note: Persistent control in privacy settings. The least urgent surface: used once consent is no longer novel.

name: Caveat
summary: Reminds people that AI output may be wrong and should be checked.
what: A short disclaimer rendered close to the input or below output: 'AI may make mistakes. Verify before use.'
why: A nearby reminder sets expectations without interrupting the task.
when: Persistent near the input. Repeated near any output that will be acted on (sent, published, deployed).
how: Keep the reminder near the input or output. Use calm language and show it once per surface.
code: ⚠ AI can make mistakes. Always verify important information before acting.

placements.note: A persistent caveat under the message box so it greets the person on every visit.
Below each panel answer: reminders sit where decisions get made.
Surfaced on hover of the generate action so it doesn't shout at the person.
Just under the inline AI prompt so the caveat travels with the cursor.
Beneath the AI-drafted reply so the person sees the caution right before sending.

variants.name: Below the input
variants.note: A quiet caption rendered just under the composer so the person sees it before sending anything.

variants.name: Output footer
variants.note: Rendered beneath an output that will be acted on: sent, deployed, published. Repeats the reminder where the risk is highest.

variants.name: Info tooltip on action
variants.note: Hover affordance on a generate button: gives the caveat without ever being in the way.

name: Avatar
summary: Uses a consistent visual mark to represent the assistant across product surfaces.
what: A non-photographic, abstract or character mark that always represents the AI in lists, message bubbles, system tray, etc.
why: A recognizable mark helps people identify the assistant across conversations and product surfaces.
when: Chat headers. Message bubbles. Any place a 'from' attribution exists.
how: Use an abstract or illustrated mark rather than a photo or well-known character. Keep it recognizable at common sizes.
code: Assistant Online

placements.note: Inside every AI message bubble so attribution is consistent down the thread.

name: Branches
summary: Lets people explore a separate conversation path without changing the original.
what: A fork action on any message that clones the conversation up to that point, opening a parallel thread the person can explore without overwriting the original.
why: Separate paths let people compare options without changing the original conversation.
when: Research, creative drafting, and debugging workflows where people need to explore multiple approaches and compare results side by side.
how: Show a branch icon on hover for every AI message; open the fork as a named sibling conversation; provide a visual indicator of which branch is active.

name: Personalization
summary: Suggests preference changes based on observed use and lets people decide whether to apply them.
what: Implicit or explicit adaptation of AI tone, format, and defaults based on observed usage patterns: surfaced as occasional opt-in prompts, never silent drift.
why: Explicit proposals let people decide whether observed preferences should become defaults.
when: Products with returning people who have established preferences (writing assistants, coding tools, personal productivity apps) after at least a few sessions.
how: Notice repeated preferences and present them as proposals the person can accept, reject, or edit.

name: Data Ownership
summary: Lets people decide whether their data can be used to improve the model.
what: A prominent, plain-language toggle that lets people opt out of their conversations being used to train or improve the model, with a clear description of what that means.
why: Clear controls help people understand and choose how their data is used.
when: Every consumer AI product: surfaced prominently during onboarding and accessible at all times in settings.
how: Default to the most privacy-protective option in enterprise contexts; explain in one sentence what 'on' and 'off' means; link to the privacy policy.

name: Incognito Mode
summary: Offers a temporary session with clear controls for history and data retention.
what: A session mode that disables all logging, memory, and history: nothing the person says in incognito is saved, used for training, or visible after the session ends.
why: A temporary session gives people more control over what appears in their history.
when: Health queries, legal questions, personal writing, financial planning: any category where people have a reasonable expectation of session-level privacy.
how: Show a persistent session indicator. Explain what is retained and for how long, using the product's confirmed policy, and keep the session out of history only when that behavior is supported.

name: Watermark
summary: Labels AI-generated content or adds provenance information to its metadata.
what: A visible label or invisible metadata marker on AI-generated outputs (images, documents, audio) that identifies the content as AI-produced.
why: Labels or metadata help preserve provenance when generated content is shared or exported.
when: Whenever the product exports or publishes AI-generated content (images, marketing copy, reports) especially in regulated industries or consumer contexts.
how: Add a small visible badge on generated outputs; embed invisible metadata for detection tools; let enterprise admins configure watermark policy.

name: Collecting Feedback
summary: Lets people rate outputs and optionally say what should improve.
what: A lightweight rating layer on every AI output (thumbs, star, or emoji) with an optional follow-up for specific feedback like 'Too long' or 'Wrong tone'.
why: Specific feedback helps identify what needs to improve in an output.
when: Every output in consumer or enterprise AI products: feedback should be a zero-friction default, not an opt-in feature.
how: Place thumbs directly under each response; offer 3–5 labeled reasons on thumbs-down; never require written explanation for a quick rating.

why: A central view helps teams manage model availability, usage, and cost.
when: Developer tools, enterprise platforms, and any product offering multiple model tiers where the person's workflow meaningfully benefits from choosing.
how: Label models by their practical strength ('Fast', 'Balanced', 'Most capable') not by internal codename; show cost difference as a relative indicator.

what: A dismissible banner, badge, or modal that tells people when the AI model, product features, or behavior have meaningfully changed since their last session.
why: Clear notices help people understand when expected behavior or available features have changed.
when: Any model upgrade, feature change, or policy update that could affect the person's established workflows or expectations.
how: Show a brief banner on first session after a change; link to a changelog or 'What's new' page; make it dismissible after one read.

when: Mature, feature-rich products (IDEs, dashboards, creative suites) where people have enough session history to reveal genuine layout preferences.
how: Offer a layout suggestion in a non-blocking card with a preview. Keep the current arrangement until accepted and provide a way to revert.
